summary: Two captives, Arthur and the narrator, talk in a cell while held by Dawna Polk, who is planning to brainwash them. Arthur admits his own moral inconsistencies and suggests Dawna's cause might have some justification, which the narrator finds unsettling. The narrator then confesses that he hurts people without much thought and does not consider himself a good person. Arthur counters that the narrator spared his life after knocking him out, and that he was still a threat, which the narrator realizes is true.
one_line: Captive narrator and Arthur debate morality in a cell, with Arthur excusing Dawna Polk's methods and the narrator confessing he is not a good person.
key_facts: Arthur says he does lots of things he is not proud of and suspects he won't weigh out well on the scales of judgment himself.
Arthur says Dawna Polk's actions are not justified but that a greater good that got out of hand makes some sense.
The narrator asks who gave Dawna Polk the right to choose in the first place.
The narrator names Courtney, Dr. Kingsley, and Reginald Kingsley as people harmed by Dawna Polk's plans.
The narrator was shaken that Arthur could see the side of the woman who had him locked up pending brainwashing.
The narrator admits he does not think a whole lot about the people he hurt.
The narrator says killing someone who threatens him has always been the smart thing to do.
The narrator says that he would have killed Arthur at the motel.
The narrator says: "I don't think I'm a very good person."
Arthur points out that the narrator knocked him out and then left him alive.
Arthur says that he was still a threat after being knocked out, and that the narrator knew it.
The narrator admits that Arthur was right, since he had expected to be in the clear but Arthur had started to become a threat.
